# Pike and shot, volley fire and drill (`pike_and_shot_drill`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs handguns_muskets; helped by close_order_infantry, standing_army_logistics, printing_press
- Core idea: Slow-loading guns give continuous fire only if the men shoot by ranks in turn: the front rank fires and files to the rear to reload while the next steps up (the countermarch), which needs six to ten ranks and endless practice. Loading is broken into numbered motions done on a word of command, taught from illustrated manuals, in small companies with many officers. Pikemen stand beside the shot to keep cavalry off while they reload. Drill also turns recruits into a unit that obeys under fire, which matters as much as the fire itself.
- Pitfalls:
  - Crediting Maurice of Nassau with inventing volley fire; Chinese texts describe earlier rotating fire, while the precise drill used at Nagashino is disputed
  - Volley fire without pikes, a ditch or wagons is ridden down by cavalry during reloading
  - Drill takes months and permanent paid units; it cannot be improvised with levies before a battle
  - The story of three neat rotating ranks at Nagashino (1575) comes from later accounts and is doubted
- History: china: 8th–11th c. – rotating crossbow volleys described in Tang and Song manuals; c. 1560 – Qi Jiguang describes arquebus volley drill; east_asia: 1575 – Nagashino, massed Japanese arquebus fire from behind palisades; islamic: 1526 – Janissary ranks fire in turn at Mohács according to some accounts; documented in the war of 1593–1606; europe: 1476–1477 – Swiss pikes destroy Burgundy; 1503 – Cerignola; 1530s – Spanish tercio; 1594 – William Louis of Nassau proposes the countermarch to Maurice from Roman models; 1607 – Jacob de Gheyn's illustrated drill book; 1630s – Gustavus Adolphus; 1683 – imperial infantry before Vienna still mixes pikes and matchlocks
- Read:
  - Geoffrey Parker, The Military Revolution (1988)
  - Jacob de Gheyn, Wapenhandelinghe van Roers, Musquetten ende Spiessen (1607)
  - Tonio Andrade, The Gunpowder Age (2016)
